title: Question 4
stem:
A progressive transverse wave travelling from left to right is shown at an instant in time in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

R and T are points on the wave.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the phase difference between the points R and T.
hints: Hint 1: Look at where R and T sit on the wave shape - R is at a crest and T is at equilibrium - and think what fraction of one complete wavelength separates them along the direction of travel.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what one full cycle means**
Think of phase as a clock for the oscillation. One full wavelength $\lambda$ corresponds to $360^{\circ}$. A crest to the next crest is $360^{\circ}$, crest to trough is half a wavelength so $180^{\circ}$.

Step 2: **Count from R to T**
Starting at crest R and moving right: R to the next trough is $\lambda/2$, then trough up to the equilibrium point T is another $\lambda/4$. Total separation is: $$ \Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{2} + \frac{\lambda}{4} = \frac{3\lambda}{4} $$ So phase difference is $3/4$ of $360^{\circ}$: $$ \phi = \frac{3}{4} \times 360^{\circ} = 270^{\circ} $$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: On Fig. 4.1, draw an arrow at point T to show the direction of movement of point T at the instant shown.

markscheme_points.text: arrow pointing vertically downwards at T

hints: Hint 1: Imagine the whole wave shape shifted a tiny distance to the right - would the string at T have to move up or down to follow the new profile, remembering particle motion is up-down for a transverse wave.
parts.proper_answer: Arrow at T pointing vertically downwards, perpendicular to direction of travel.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember particles do not travel with the wave**
In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to energy travel. Here energy goes left to right, so point T can only move vertically up or down.

Step 2: **Slide the wave a little to the right**
A short time later the whole sine shape has moved right. At the position of T, the part of the wave just to the left (which is lower, coming out of the trough) will arrive. So T must move down to meet it. That is why you draw a short vertical arrow down at T.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The horizontal distance between R and T is $0.62\text{ cm}$, as shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2 (not to scale)

The speed of the wave is $0.27\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate the frequency of the wave.

markscheme_points.text: v = fλ or v = λ / T and f = 1 / T

hints: Hint 1: Use your result from (a) to express the 0.62 cm distance as a fraction of one full wavelength - what fraction of $\lambda$ is the R to T separation.
Hint 2: Rearrange that fraction to find one full $\lambda$ in cm, then convert it to metres for use with the wave speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
Hint 3: Link speed, frequency and wavelength together to solve for frequency, checking your final value is in Hz to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Turn the 0.62 cm into a full wavelength**
From (a) the R to T distance is $3/4$ of a wavelength: $$ \frac{3}{4}\lambda = 0.62 \text{ cm} $$ So: $$ \lambda = 0.62 \times \frac{4}{3} = 0.827 \text{ cm} $$ In metres: $$ \lambda = 0.827 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 8.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} $$ A common slip is to use 0.62 cm directly as $\lambda$. Always check the fraction first.

Step 2: **Apply the wave equation**
For any progressive wave: $$ v = f\lambda $$ Rearranged for frequency: $$ f = \frac{v}{\lambda} $$

Step 3: **Calculate the frequency**
Insert $v = 0.27 \text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$ f = \frac{0.27}{8.27 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 32.6 \text{ Hz} $$ To 2 significant figures: $$ f \approx 33 \text{ Hz} $$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
The wave is a water wave produced by a dipper $S_1$ attached to a vibrator in a ripple tank.

An identical dipper $S_2$ is attached to the same vibrator. The two dippers produce an interference pattern on the water in the tank, as shown in Fig. 4.3.

{{figure:figure_4_3}}

Fig. 4.3 (not to scale)

The wave crests from each source are represented by solid lines on Fig. 4.3 and the wave troughs are represented by dashed lines.

At point P in Fig. 4.3, the wave from $S_1$ has the same amplitude $A$ as the wave from $S_2$.

Describe and explain the amplitude of the resultant wave at point P.

markscheme_points.text: resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements of the waves or waves (from S1 and S2) superpose (at P)

Any one point from: • (at P) the waves (from the two sources) (always) destructive and a half wavelengths • (at P) the waves have a path difference that is (always) an odd number of half wavelengths • (at P) the waves have a phase difference that is (always) 180° out of phase with the other wave
amplitude (of the resultant wave) is zero (at all times)

hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling what happens when two waves meet at the same point - how do their individual displacements combine to give the resultant displacement.

Hint 2: Look closely at Fig. 4.3 at point P - is a solid crest line meeting another solid crest line, or is a solid line meeting a dashed line, and what does that tell you about crest-trough alignment.
Hint 3: Translate that crest-trough alignment into path difference or phase difference language and think what resultant amplitude that gives if both waves have amplitude $A$.
parts.proper_answer: Resultant amplitude is zero. By superposition, resultant displacement is sum of individual displacements. At P a crest from one source meets a trough from the other, so path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths and phase difference is $180^{\circ}$. The waves cancel at all times giving destructive interference.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the superposition idea**
When two waves arrive at the same place, you add their displacements vectorially at every instant: $$ x_{resultant} = x_1 + x_2 $$ This is the principle of superposition. It holds at P for the wave from $S_1$ and the wave from $S_2$.

Step 2: **Spot what meets at P**
Solid lines are crests (maximum positive displacement $+A$) and dashed lines are troughs (maximum negative displacement $-A$). At P a solid line from one source crosses a dashed line from the other source. So a crest always meets a trough there.

Step 3: **Explain why cancellation is permanent**
Crest meeting trough means the two waves are always $180^{\circ}$ out of phase at P. In distance terms the path difference $S_1P - S_2P$ is an odd number of half wavelengths: $$ \text{path difference} = (n + 1/2)\lambda $$ So $+A$ plus $-A$ gives: $$ A_{resultant} = A - A = 0 $$ The amplitude stays zero at all times. This is destructive interference, forming a minimum or nodal line.
